title: MATH GAOKAO - 13
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a proposition from an open sentence.
questions.question: Which of the following is a proposition?
questions.explanation: A proposition is a declarative statement that has a definite truth value, either true or false. The statement \(2+3=6\) is false, but it is still a proposition because its truth value is definite. The statement \(x+2=5\) depends on the value of \(x\), so it is an open sentence, not a proposition.
questions.hint: Recall that a proposition must be either true or false without depending on a variable.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a conjunction and a disjunction.
questions.question: Let \(p\): \(5>2\), and let \(q\): \(7\) is even. Which compound statement is false?
questions.explanation:
The statement \(p\) is true because \(5>2\). The statement \(q\) is false because \(7\) is odd, not even. For the conjunction,
\[
p\land q
\]
is true only if both \(p\) and \(q\) are true. Since \(q\) is false, \(p\land q\) is false. For the disjunction,
\[
p\lor q
\]
is true because at least one of \(p\) and \(q\) is true.
questions.hint: Check the truth value of each simple statement first, then apply the rules for \(\land\) and \(\lor\).

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of a universally quantified statement.
questions.question: What is the negation of the statement “All real numbers \(x\) satisfy \(x^2\ge 0\)”?
questions.explanation:
The negation of a universal statement
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ P(x)
\]
is the existential statement
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\ \neg P(x).
\]
Here \(P(x)\) is \(x^2\ge 0\), so \(\neg P(x)\) is \(x^2<0\). Therefore, the negation is
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\ x^2<0.
\]
questions.hint: Negating “for all” changes it to “there exists” and negates the inner condition.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a statement logically equivalent to a given conditional statement.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to “If a number is divisible by \(4\), then it is even”?

options.label: A
options.text: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by \(4\).

options.label: B
options.text: If a number is even, then it is divisible by \(4\).

questions.explanation:
For a conditional statement \(p\rightarrow q\), the contrapositive is
\[
\neg q\rightarrow \neg p,
\]
and it is logically equivalent to the original statement. Here \(p\) is “a number is divisible by \(4\)” and \(q\) is “a number is even.” Therefore, the contrapositive is “If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by \(4\).” Option B is the converse, which is not logically equivalent in general.
questions.hint: Use the contrapositive, not the converse.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a conditional statement in terms of sufficient and necessary conditions.
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), consider the statement “If \(n\) is divisible by \(6\), then \(n\) is divisible by \(3\).” Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Divisibility by \(6\) is sufficient for divisibility by \(3\).

options.label: B
options.text: Divisibility by \(6\) is necessary for divisibility by \(3\).

questions.explanation: In a conditional statement \(p\rightarrow q\), \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\). Here \(p\) is “\(n\) is divisible by \(6\)” and \(q\) is “\(n\) is divisible by \(3\).” Since every integer divisible by \(6\) is also divisible by \(3\), divisibility by \(6\) is sufficient for divisibility by \(3\). It is not necessary, because \(3\) itself is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(6\).
questions.hint: In \(p\rightarrow q\), the condition \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\), while \(q\) is necessary for \(p\).

questions.learningObjective: Apply De Morgan’s law to negate a compound statement.
questions.question: What is the negation of “\(x>0\) and \(y<0\)”?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan’s law, the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations:
\[
\neg(p\land q)\equiv \neg p\lor \neg q.
\]
Here \(p\) is \(x>0\), so \(\neg p\) is \(x\le 0\). Also \(q\) is \(y<0\), so \(\neg q\) is \(y\ge 0\). Therefore, the negation is
\[
x\le 0\ \text{or}\ y\ge 0.
\]
questions.hint: Negate each part and change “and” to “or.”

questions.learningObjective: Negate a universal conditional statement involving integers.
questions.question: What is the negation of “For every integer \(n\), if \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even”?

options.label: A
options.text: For every integer \(n\), \(n\) is even and \(n^2\) is even.

options.label: B
options.text: There exists an integer \(n\) such that \(n\) is even and \(n^2\) is odd.

questions.explanation:
The original statement has the form
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb{Z},\ (P(n)\rightarrow Q(n)),
\]
where \(P(n)\) is “\(n\) is even” and \(Q(n)\) is “\(n^2\) is even.” The negation of a universal statement is an existential statement, and the negation of \(P\rightarrow Q\) is \(P\land \neg Q\). Therefore, the negation is
\[
\exists n\in\mathbb{Z},\ (P(n)\land \neg Q(n)).
\]
That is, there exists an integer \(n\) such that \(n\) is even and \(n^2\) is not even. For an integer, “not even” means odd. Hence the negation is: There exists an integer \(n\) such that \(n\) is even and \(n^2\) is odd.
questions.hint: Negate the universal quantifier first, then negate the conditional inside.

questions.concept: Truth Values with a Finite Domain
questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of quantified statements over a finite set.
questions.question: Let \(D=\{1,2,3\}\). Which statement is false?
questions.explanation:
Check statement A: for \(x=1\), \(1+2=3<6\); for \(x=2\), \(2+2=4<6\); for \(x=3\), \(3+2=5<6\). Thus A is true for every element of \(D\).
Check statement B: the equation \(x+3=7\) gives \(x=4\). But \(4\notin D\), so no element of \(D\) satisfies \(x+3=7\). Therefore, B is false.
questions.hint: Test each element of the finite domain \(D\) for both statements.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a statement equivalent to an implication.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
The implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. The statement \(\neg p\lor q\) is also false only when \(\neg p\) is false and \(q\) is false, that is, when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Therefore,
\[
p\rightarrow q\equiv \neg p\lor q.
\]
The statement \(q\rightarrow p\) is the converse, which is not logically equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\) in general.
questions.hint: Recall that an implication can be rewritten using “not \(p\) or \(q\).”
